summary: Round 2, scoped to the three round-1 fixes. Two of the three are genuinely closed, verified by mutation rather than by reading: replacing the round trip with `return true` (as `return sequence >= 0 || true;`) now FAILS LogKeysTest.aKeyWhoseDigitsParseButDoNotRegenerateIsRefused, where before it left the suite green; and `CommitLog.isEntryKey` is deleted with no remaining caller anywhere in the tree (grep over all *.java finds only LogKeys' definition, its two ChainReplay call sites and LogKeysTest). CommitLog's remaining delegation is coherent -- `keys` is still read by `keyFor` and `logPrefix`, the two production LIST sites both go through `LogKeys` directly, and CommitLog itself issues no `list` at all, so nothing needed the deleted delegate. Every JDK claim the new T0 test makes was checked against a real run, not assumed: `Long.parseUnsignedLong("+000000000000009", 16)` does yield 9 (a leading plus is accepted, a leading minus is not), the seventeen-digit form does yield 9, uppercase yields 10, and all four regenerate to something other than the candidate. `keyFor(Long.MAX_VALUE)` is `7fffffffffffffff.delta` and does round-trip, so that assertion is correct; it is not reachable by a real writer (sequence advances by one per commit from 0) but it is the correct boundary for 'keys the writer produces', so the assertion is sound rather than over-claimed. The backlog row's `return false` figure is honest -- measured 32 sequencer failures, exactly as claimed -- and the tree is green at 741 tests, also as claimed. No request-rate change: the delta since round 1 is a javadoc paragraph, a deletion and a test, and adds no get/put/list/stat. The third fix is the one that does not hold up, and it is filed below as a minor. Two observations that are NOT findings, recorded so they are not lost rather than because they block: (1) the round trip admits the whole unsigned range, because `%016x` formats a long unsigned -- `<logPrefix>ffffffffffffffff.delta` regenerates byte-identically and is accepted, so the allow-list is over all 2^64 keys of the shape rather than over the keys a writer can produce; there is no producer of such a key today, so under `failure-scenario` it is a style opinion, not a defect. (2) the `LogKeys keys` field added by the split is shadowed by a pre-existing `Set<String> keys` local in CommitLog's submission validation -- round-1 surface, already carrying a verdict, named only because I read past it.

findings.title: The new ChainReplay javadoc paragraph justifies the `CommitLog` leftover with a check that cannot fire
findings.detail: The paragraph added to close round-1 finding 3 says of `firstEntry`: 'That constructor VALIDATES the epoch, and the walks reaching it arrive by decrementing, so swapping it for a bare LogKeys would drop the check on the one path that can go negative.' The first clause is true -- `CommitLog`'s constructor throws IllegalArgumentException on `epoch < 0`. The operative clause is false: there is no check to drop, because the check can never execute at this site. `firstEntry` has exactly two callers, and both guard the argument in the same expression. `replayAncestry` calls it as the first statement inside `while (chainEpoch >= 1)`. `firstInheritableAncestor` calls it inside `while (chainEpoch >= 1 && neverOpened(firstEntry(store, prefix, chainEpoch), atOrigin))`, where `&&` short-circuits. The walks can indeed go non-positive -- `chainEpoch = chainEpoch - 1` in the neverOpened branch, `chainEpoch--` in firstInheritableAncestor, and `chainEpoch = opening.prevEpoch()` where the corruption test only bounds prevEpoch from ABOVE, so a decoded negative prevEpoch passes it -- but in every one of those three cases the loop condition is re-evaluated before the next call and ends the walk. The constructor never sees the negative value. Measured: replacing `new CommitLog(store, prefix, chainEpoch).keyFor(0)` with `new LogKeys(prefix, chainEpoch).keyFor(0)` in `firstEntry` leaves all 741 tests green, in a fresh copy of the staged bytes. Failure scenario, which is why this is filed rather than shrugged at: the paragraph was written to close a finding about a leftover dependency, and it does not close it -- it promotes the leftover to a documented invariant. This file's own `neverOpened` javadoc already names the changes coming to these exact walks ('any future path that opens without sealing first -- M4.6d's rerouting or M5's forwarding', and M4.23 for the origin gap), and closing M4.23's gap means loosening precisely the `chainEpoch >= 1` guard that is the real and only protection here. A maintainer doing that will read this paragraph, believe the constructor still guards the negative case, and remove the guard that actually does. Meanwhile the file keeps constructing a WRITER to ask a naming question, which is what the same file's javadoc two paragraphs above -- 'ADDRESSING COMES FROM LogKeys, never re-derived here' -- asserts it does not do. The honest forms are either to move `firstEntry` to `LogKeys` and delete the paragraph, or to keep the call and say plainly that it is a leftover of the split rather than a guard. Note that the deletion is three sentences of prose removed and none added, so the usual `minors-land` argument against fixing a minor (that the fix creates the next round's surface) does not apply with its normal force here -- but it is a comment either way, nothing behaves differently, and under `minors-land` it lands as recorded. It does NOT block.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.23 (or M5's forwarding, which this file's own neverOpened javadoc names) loosens the `chainEpoch >= 1` loop guard in `firstInheritableAncestor`/`replayAncestry` so the walk can reach the origin. The maintainer doing it reads this paragraph, believes `CommitLog`'s constructor still rejects a negative epoch at `firstEntry`, and removes the guard that was in fact the only one. `firstEntry` then formats `%016x` of a negative epoch into a legal-looking key -- e.g. epoch -1 becomes `ffffffffffffffff`, which sorts ABOVE every real epoch -- STATs it, gets empty, and the ancestry walk silently ends one hop early or loops on a slot no writer owns, so a taking-over leader inherits no offsets and reassigns from 0. That is I2, arrived at through a comment that said the check was there.
